name: Space & the Planets - very easy (AI-written, not yet reviewed)
description: 17 very easy questions on space and the planets, written by Claude on 2026-10-06 as the gentlest level of the 'Space & the Planets' review pack: things almost everyone knows, in one short plain sentence, worded for adults. They are marked easy with a note "very easy" until the very easy level lands. The fact-check judged 2 of them merely easy and took off their note, so the pack is 15 very easy, 2 easy. The independent fact-check kept 17 of 17 written, fixed 3 and deleted 0. Every question and answer needs checking by a person before anybody plays it.

source.name: Written by hand by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) on 2026-10-06, from its own knowledge plus the pages each item cites: no API call. 16 items cite a page the writing pass fetched on 2026-10-06 and quote the phrase on it that supports the fact; 1 rest on "common knowledge" (genuinely universal everyday facts), each with the reason. Then fact-checked item by item by a separate Claude pass on 2026-10-06 that did not write them (every cited page re-fetched and read for the fact, every answer, wrong answer, explanation and level checked; `checked` keeps who checked it and what was fixed; items that could not be made right, and duplicates of other packs, were deleted). Very easy items are marked difficulty "easy" with "note": "very easy" until the very easy level lands. A person still reviews it by playing.

review.how: Check every question, answer and explanation. Fix or delete what is wrong, set status to 'reviewed' with your name and the date, then move the file to packs/ and list it in pack_library.js.

items.question: Which of these is the biggest?
items.explain: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth.

source.title: Wikipedia: Sun
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'It is the largest and most massive object in the Solar System' and 'around 109 times that of Earth'.

items.question: Where does moonlight really come from?
items.explain: The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight.

source.title: NASA Science: Moon Phases
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'The Moon does not make its own light' and 'Moonlight" is actually reflected sunlight'.

checked.fixed: level very easy -> easy (most adults know the Moon reflects sunlight, but it is not instant for nearly everyone)

items.question: What do we call the Moon when it looks like a complete bright circle?
items.explain: The Moon's cycle of phases repeats about every 29.5 days.

source.title: NASA Science: Moon Phases
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'full Moon' and 'The cycle repeats about once a month (every 29.5 days)'.

items.question: What do astronauts ride to blast off into space?
items.explain: A rocket carries its own fuel and needs no outside air to fly.

source.title: Wikipedia: Rocket
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'uses a rocket engine to accelerate without using any surrounding air' and 'fuelled entirely by propellant which they carry'.

items.question: About how long does Earth take to spin around once?
items.explain: That spin is why each place has morning, afternoon, evening and night.

source.title: Wikipedia: Day
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'A day is the time period of a full rotation of the Earth with respect to the Sun' and 'experiences morning , afternoon , evening , and night'.

checked.fixed: level very easy -> easy (spin = day is easily confused with orbit = year; most adults, not nearly everyone)

items.question: What do astronauts wear to work outside their spacecraft?
items.explain: A spacesuit supplies oxygen and protects against extreme heat and cold.

source.title: Wikipedia: Space suit
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'For extravehicular activity (EVA), more complex space suits are worn' and 'Supply of breathable oxygen' and 'protects against temperature extremes'.

items.question: Which tool helps people see faraway stars and planets?
items.explain: Galileo built his own telescope in 1609 to study the night sky.

source.title: Wikipedia: Telescope
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Galileo heard about it and, in 1609, built his own version, and made his telescopic observations of celestial objects'.

items.question: What is the long glowing trail behind a comet called?
items.explain: A comet's tail points away from the Sun.

source.title: Wikipedia: Comet
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'an enormous "tail" to form pointing away from the Sun'.

items.question: Compared with Earth, how big is the Moon?
items.explain: The Moon is roughly one-quarter as wide as Earth.

source.title: Wikipedia: Moon
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'its diameter is 3,474 km (2,159 mi) , roughly one-quarter of Earth's'.

items.question: How many moons does Earth have?
items.explain: Our Moon is the fifth largest moon in the solar system.

source.title: Wikipedia: Moon
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'The Moon is the only natural satellite of Earth' and 'The Moon is the fifth largest (by size and mass) natural satellite of the Solar System'.

items.question: What are the round hollows on the Moon's surface called?
items.explain: Craters formed when asteroids and comets struck the Moon.

source.title: Wikipedia: Moon
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'craters formed when asteroids and comets collide with the lunar surface'.

items.question: Which country's flag did astronauts plant on the Moon?
items.explain: Six American flags were planted during the Apollo Moon landings.

source.title: Wikipedia: Lunar Flag Assembly
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'a kit containing a flag of the United States designed to be erected on the Moon' and 'Six such flag assemblies were planted on the Moon'.

items.question: What did Apollo astronauts bring back from the Moon?
items.explain: Six Apollo missions brought home about 840 pounds of Moon samples.

source.title: Wikipedia: Moon rock
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'Six Apollo missions collected 2,200 samples of material weighing 381 kilograms (840 lb)'.

items.question: Which agency runs the American space program?
items.explain: NASA stands for National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

source.title: Wikipedia: NASA
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the fact-check pass; the page text contains: 'The National Aeronautics and Space Administration ( NASA' and 'responsible for the United States' civil space program'.

checked.fixed: distractors NFL/NBA/PBS (sports leagues, TV network) -> IRS/USPS/EPA (same kind: US agencies); note now quotes the 'civil space program' line instead of seal alt-text

items.question: What shape is Earth?
items.explain: Photos taken from space show Earth as a round blue ball.

source.note: Universally known: Earth is round, as photos from space show; no citation needed.

items.question: What do we call the Sun and the planets that go around it?
items.explain: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago.

source.title: Wikipedia: Solar System
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'The Solar System is the gravitationally bound system of the Sun and the masses that orbit it' and 'The system formed about 4.6 billion years ago'.

items.question: What do we call the path a planet follows around the Sun?
items.explain: Planet orbits are slightly stretched circles called ellipses.

source.title: Wikipedia: Orbit
source.note: Fetched 2026-10-06 by the writing pass; the page text contains: 'an orbit is the curved trajectory of an object' and 'planets, and satellites follow elliptic orbits'.
